question: What is object storage, and how is it different from file storage and block storage?
answer_hinglish:
Teeno storage ke alag levels hain. Block storage sabse neeche hai: disk ko fixed-size blocks mein dekhte ho, upar OS ka filesystem ya database chalta hai (EBS volume, DB disk). File storage uske upar hai: directory tree, POSIX operations -- open, seek, rename, file ke beech mein likhna. Object storage alag model hai: bucket + key + bytes + metadata, aur access HTTP API se hota hai -- poora object PUT, poora (ya range) GET, DELETE.

Sabse bada farak update ka hai. File mein aap byte 500 pe jaake overwrite kar sakte ho. Object mein nahi -- naya object likhte ho jo purane ko replace karta hai (versioning ho toh naya version). Isi immutability ki wajah se object storage practically unlimited scale karta hai: koi locking-within-file nahi, koi directory tree consistency nahi, sirf flat key -> blob mapping.

Object storage mein metadata bhi rich hota hai: content type, user metadata (`x-obj-meta-*`), ETag, versions. Use cases: backups, images/videos, data lakes, static assets. Block storage DB volumes ke liye, file storage shared drives ke liye.

Mere Project 7 mein maine S3 jaisa object store banaya hai -- buckets, objects, versions, multipart, presigned URLs -- aur `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` mein yahi comparison table hai. Interview mein main yeh line bolta hoon: "object storage = immutable objects in a flat namespace over HTTP; isliye cheap aur horizontally scalable, lekin in-place edit aur rename jaise POSIX features nahi."
why_needed: Interview mein almost har storage discussion yahin se shuru hoti hai; sahi tool choose karne ke liye teeno ka model samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Block storage = khaali zameen ke plot (aap jo chaho banao). File storage = ek building jisme floors aur rooms (folders) hain. Object storage = ek bada warehouse jahan har box pe ek unique label (key) hai -- box ke andar kuch badalna ho toh naya box rakh do.
how_it_works: Object store do cheezein rakhta hai: metadata (key, size, etag, version, permissions) aur bytes. Client HTTP verbs use karta hai. Server key ko metadata index mein dhoondhta hai aur bytes blob store se stream karta hai. Koi partial overwrite nahi hota, isliye concurrency sirf 'kaunsa version latest hai' tak simit rehti hai.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` mein Block/File/Object table hai. Code mein yeh model `services/objects.py` mein dikhta hai: `put_object` hamesha naya blob likhta hai (`new_blob_key()`) aur `commit_version` naya row insert karta hai -- koi in-place update of bytes nahi hai. API `api/routes.py` mein HTTP verbs pe hai: `PUT/GET/HEAD/DELETE /buckets/{b}/objects/{key}`.
advantages: HTTP API -> kahin se bhi access
disadvantages: Rename = copy (S3 mein); latency file system se zyada
POSIX apps directly use nahi kar sakte
common_mistakes: Object storage ko network file system samajh lena
Sochna ki 'folders' real hain
DB volume ke liye object storage use karna

question: Object storage has a flat namespace. How do 'folders' work then?
answer_hinglish:
Folders ek illusion hain. `docs/2026/report.pdf` ek single key hai -- system mein koi `docs` directory object exist nahi karta. Listing API `prefix` aur `delimiter` parameters se folder jaisa view banati hai.

Example: keys hain `a.txt`, `docs/1.txt`, `docs/2.txt`, `docs/sub/3.txt`, `img/x.png`. Agar aap `delimiter=/` ke saath list karo bina prefix ke, toh jo keys mein prefix ke baad `/` aata hai unko group kar dete hain: result `contents = [a.txt]`, `common_prefixes = [docs/, img/]`. Phir `prefix=docs/&delimiter=/` -> `contents = [docs/1.txt, docs/2.txt]`, `common_prefixes = [docs/sub/]`. UI isi ko folder tree ki tarah dikhata hai.

Isse do baatein follow hoti hain. Pehli: 'folder rename' cheap nahi hai real S3 mein -- har key ko copy + delete karna padta hai. Doosri: khaali folder exist nahi kar sakta (S3 console zero-byte `folder/` object bana ke fake karta hai).

Mere project mein `list_objects` ListObjectsV2 semantics follow karta hai, aur `test_listing_prefix_delimiter_pagination` exactly upar wale keys ke saath yahi assert karta hai. Implementation mein ek chhota trick hai: jab ek common prefix mil jaye, toh hum us 'folder' ke andar ki saari keys skip karne ke liye `after = cp + '\U0010ffff'` set karte hain, taaki ek folder mein million keys ho tab bhi hum unhe ek ek karke scan na karein.
why_needed: Users aur tools folder hierarchy expect karte hain; flat namespace pe yeh view efficiently banana listing API ka kaam hai.
real_world_analogy: Library mein saari books ek lambi shelf pe alphabetical order mein hain; 'History/' wala section sirf isliye dikhta hai kyunki un sab ke labels 'History/' se shuru hote hain -- koi alag almirah nahi hai.
how_it_works: Server prefix match karta hai (`key LIKE 'prefix%'`), har key ka prefix ke baad ka hissa dekhta hai; agar usme delimiter hai toh `prefix + first_segment + delimiter` common prefix ban jata hai aur us range ki baaki keys skip ho jati hain. Results key order mein aate hain, `max_keys` pe truncate hote hain aur `next_start_after` pagination cursor deta hai.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py::list_objects` -- `rest = r['key'][len(prefix):]`; agar `delimiter in rest` toh `cp = prefix + rest.split(delimiter, 1)[0] + delimiter` aur `after = skipped_to = cp + '\U0010ffff'`. Index `ix_objects_list (bucket, key text_pattern_ops) WHERE is_latest AND NOT is_delete_marker` prefix scan ko fast banata hai. Test: `test_listing_prefix_delimiter_pagination` (`common_prefixes == ['docs/', 'img/']`).
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (list_objects)
rest = r["key"][len(prefix):]
if delimiter and delimiter in rest:
    cp = prefix + rest.split(delimiter, 1)[0] + delimiter
    prefixes.append(cp)
    after = skipped_to = cp + "\U0010ffff"   # jump past every key under this "folder"
    break
contents.append(dict(r))
after = r["key"]
advantages: Folder view on-demand compute hota hai
disadvantages: Listing pe hi load aata hai

Delimiter ke bina listing mein folders expect karna
Pagination cursor ke bina saari keys ek saath fetch karna

question: Explain the bucket, key, and version model of this object store.
answer_hinglish:
Teen level hain. Bucket ek top-level container hai jiska owner hota hai aur jispe config lagti hai: versioning, ACL (public_read + grants), quota, lifecycle rules. Bucket ke andar key ek string hai (1 se 1024 bytes) jo object ko identify karti hai. Aur har key ke multiple versions ho sakte hain; har version ek row hai jisme size, etag, sha256, content type, user metadata aur blob_key hota hai.

Bucket names DNS-compatible hone chahiye: 3-63 chars, lowercase, digits, dot, hyphen -- yeh rule database ke CHECK constraint mein hai `name ~ '^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]{1,61}[a-z0-9]$'`. Galat naam pe `create_bucket` IntegrityError pakad ke 422 deta hai, duplicate pe 409 `BucketAlreadyExists`. Bucket delete tabhi hota hai jab koi version (old versions bhi) aur koi in-progress multipart upload na ho -- warna 409 `BucketNotEmpty`.

Version id ka ek special case: jab versioning kabhi enable nahi hua, version_id literal string `'null'` hai (S3 semantics). Enabled bucket mein har PUT `uuid4().hex` version id leta hai. Response mein `x-obj-version-id` header aata hai, aur GET `?versionId=` se purana version padh sakte ho.

Key sirf data hai -- `../../etc/passwd` bhi valid key hai, kyunki bytes us naam se kabhi disk pe nahi jaate; random blob key use hoti hai.
why_needed: Permissions, quotas aur lifecycle bucket level pe lagte hain; versions recoverability dete hain. Model clear ho tabhi API design samajh aata hai.
real_world_analogy: Bucket = ek godown, key = shelf pe label, version = us label ke peeche rakhe purane boxes ka stack jisme sabse upar wala current hai.
how_it_works: Postgres mein `buckets` table (name PK, owner_key, versioning, public_read, quota_bytes) aur `objects` table (bucket, key, version_id, is_latest, is_delete_marker, ...). Ek key ke saare versions same (bucket, key) share karte hain; `is_latest` batata hai kaunsa current hai.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py`: buckets CHECK constraint, `versioning IN ('disabled','enabled','suspended')`, objects `UNIQUE (bucket, key, version_id)`. `api/routes.py::_check_key` key ko 1..1024 bytes check karta hai; `create_bucket` IntegrityError ko 422/409 mein map karta hai; `delete_bucket` objects aur multipart_uploads dono check karta hai. Test: `test_bucket_rules` (`Bad_Name` -> 422, duplicate -> 409, non-empty delete -> 409).
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: migrations/versions/0001_initial.py
name text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (name ~ '^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]{1,61}[a-z0-9]$'),
versioning text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'disabled'
  CHECK (versioning IN ('disabled', 'enabled', 'suspended')),
...
version_id text NOT NULL,   -- 'null' when versioning was never enabled
UNIQUE (bucket, key, version_id)
advantages: DB constraints galat data ko andar aane hi nahi dete
disadvantages: Bucket names global/unique hone se naming conflicts
common_mistakes: Key ko file path samajhna
Bucket delete karte waqt old versions bhool jana
version_id ko NULL (SQL) samajhna -- yahan string 'null' hai

question: What is an ETag and what is it used for?
answer_hinglish:
ETag ek identifier hai jo object ke content ko represent karta hai. Simple PUT ke liye mere system mein ETag = body ka MD5 hex, quotes ke saath header mein: `ETag: "5d41..."`. Iske do kaam hain.

Pehla, integrity: client upload ke baad apna local MD5 compare kar sakta hai -- match hua toh bytes sahi pahunche. (Upload ke waqt `Content-MD5` header bhejna aur better hai, kyunki tab server khud mismatch pe 400 BadDigest de deta hai aur kuch commit hi nahi hota.)

Doosra, caching: client GET ke saath `If-None-Match: "<etag>"` bhejta hai. Agar current version ka ETag same hai, server 304 Not Modified deta hai, body nahi bhejta -- bandwidth bachi. `test_range_requests_and_conditional_get` yahi check karta hai.

Ek important gotcha: multipart upload ka ETag MD5 nahi hota. Woh `md5(saare parts ke binary md5 concat) + '-N'` hota hai. Isliye ETag ko 'object ka MD5' maan ke end-to-end verification karna galat hai. Isi wajah se main har object ka SHA-256 bhi store karta hoon (`x-obj-checksum-sha256` header) -- woh hamesha poore content ka hota hai, multipart mein bhi.

ETag streaming ke dauraan hi `HashingStream` compute karta hai, toh extra pass nahi lagta.
why_needed: Clients ko change detection aur integrity check ke liye ek sasta content fingerprint chahiye; CDNs aur browsers bhi ETag se cache validate karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Parcel ki seal number: aap receive karte waqt number match karo -- same hai toh parcel kisi ne khola nahi; aur agar dukaandaar bole 'same seal number wala parcel aapke paas already hai' toh dobara bhejne ki zaroorat nahi.
how_it_works: Upload stream hote waqt md5 update hota hai; end mein hexdigest ETag ban jata hai aur `objects.etag` column mein store hota hai. GET pe `_object_headers` usse quote karke bhejta hai. `If-None-Match` ko `strip('"')` karke compare kiya jata hai.
in_this_project: `storage/base.py::HashingStream` md5 compute karta hai; `put_object` `etag=info.md5` store karta hai; `routes.py::put_object` response mein `ETag: "{res.etag}"`. `get_object` mein: `if if_none_match and if_none_match.strip('"') == row['etag']: return Response(status_code=304, ...)`. Multipart ETag `complete_multipart` mein banta hai. Tests: `test_put_get_roundtrip_metadata_and_etag`, `test_range_requests_and_conditional_get`, `test_multipart_upload`.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/api/routes.py (get_object)
headers = _object_headers(row)
if if_none_match and if_none_match.strip('"') == row["etag"]:
    return Response(status_code=304, headers={"ETag": headers["ETag"]})   # client cache is still valid
disadvantages: MD5 cryptographically weak hai (adversarial collision possible)
common_mistakes: Multipart object ka ETag local MD5 se compare karna
ETag ke quotes strip na karna
ETag ko security signature samajhna

question: Why can't you modify part of an object in place, and what happens on overwrite?
answer_hinglish:
Object storage mein objects immutable hain: ek baar likha toh bytes kabhi badalte nahi. 'Edit' ka matlab hai naya object PUT karna jo purane ko replace kare. Yeh limitation nahi, design choice hai -- isi se system simple aur scalable banta hai: koi byte-range locking nahi, readers ko kabhi half-updated object nahi dikhta, caching aasaan (same version = same bytes forever).

Mere system mein overwrite ka flow: `put_object` hamesha ek NAYA random blob likhta hai -- purane blob ko kabhi touch nahi karta. Phir short transaction mein metadata flip hota hai. Agar bucket versioning disabled hai toh `'null'` version wala purana row delete hota hai aur uska blob `blob_deletions` queue mein jaata hai (GC baad mein delete karega). Agar versioning enabled hai toh purana row `is_latest = false` ho jata hai aur naya row latest ban jata hai -- purana version `?versionId=` se ab bhi readable hai.

Iska fayda: commit se pehle tak readers purana version dekhte hain, commit ke baad naya -- beech ki koi state visible nahi. Aur agar upload beech mein fail ho jaye toh purana object bilkul safe hai.

Test `test_unversioned_overwrite_queues_old_blob` check karta hai ki overwrite ke baad sirf 1 row bachi aur 1 blob deletion queue mein hai. Agar kisi ko sach mein append chahiye (logs), toh object storage mein pattern hai naye objects likhna (`logs/2026-11-17/part-0001`) ya multipart.
why_needed: Immutability ki wajah se readers ko consistent bytes milte hain, caching safe hota hai aur concurrency sirf metadata pe handle karni padti hai.
real_world_analogy: Printed book mein typo theek nahi karte -- naya edition chhapte ho; purana edition library mein reh sakta hai (versioning) ya raddi mein jaata hai (unversioned overwrite).
how_it_works: Write = naya blob + metadata pointer swap. Pointer swap ek DB transaction mein atomic hai. Purane blob ko asynchronously reclaim kiya jata hai.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py::put_object` -> `new_blob_key()` -> `storage.put` -> `commit_version`. Disabled/suspended mein `commit_version` null row DELETE + `_queue_blob_deletion(s, null_row.blob_key)`; enabled mein `UPDATE objects SET is_latest = false`. Test: `test_unversioned_overwrite_queues_old_blob` (count(objects)=1, count(blob_deletions)=1).
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (commit_version, unversioned branch)
version_id = "null"
null_row = (await s.execute(text("SELECT id, blob_key, is_latest FROM objects WHERE bucket = :b AND key = :k "
                                 "AND version_id = 'null'"), {...})).first()
if null_row:
    await s.execute(text("DELETE FROM objects WHERE id = :i"), {"i": null_row.id})
    await _queue_blob_deletion(s, null_row.blob_key)

Failed upload purane object ko kharab nahi karta

question: How do range requests (206, 416) and conditional GET (If-None-Match, 304) work here?
answer_hinglish:
Range request mein client poora object nahi, sirf ek byte range maangta hai: `Range: bytes=100-199`. Server 206 Partial Content deta hai, `Content-Range: bytes 100-199/25600` header ke saath. Isse download resume hota hai (99% pe network gaya toh sirf baaki maango) aur bade files parallel chunks mein download ho sakte hain. Video players bhi seek ke liye yahi use karte hain.

Mera `parse_range` teen forms support karta hai: `bytes=0-99`, `bytes=100-` (100 se end tak), `bytes=-50` (last 50 bytes). End size se bada ho toh clamp hota hai. Agar start object size se bada ho (`bytes=99999-` on 25600 bytes) toh 416 Range Not Satisfiable (`InvalidRange`). Multi-range (`bytes=0-1,5-6`) support nahi hai -- 416 deta hai.

Conditional GET: client ke paas cached copy hai, woh `If-None-Match: "<etag>"` bhejta hai. Agar current version ka ETag same hai, server 304 Not Modified, bina body. Note karo order: `get_object` pehle 304 check karta hai, phir range parse karta hai.

Storage layer tak range jaati hai: local adapter `f.seek(start)` karke sirf zaroori bytes padhta hai, S3 adapter `Range` header ke saath `get_object` karta hai -- toh 1GB object ka 100 bytes maangne pe 1GB read nahi hota.

Limitation (observation): sirf single ETag wala If-None-Match hai; If-Match, If-Modified-Since, `*` support nahi.
why_needed: Large objects ke liye resume, parallel download aur seek zaroori hain; conditional GET bandwidth aur latency bachata hai.
real_world_analogy: Range = poori kitaab ki jagah sirf page 100-199 ki photocopy maangna. 304 = 'aapke paas jo edition hai wahi latest hai, naya mat le jao'.
how_it_works: Server metadata se size jaanta hai, range validate karta hai, phir adapter ko (start, end) deta hai. Response 206 + Content-Range + Content-Length (end-start+1). ETag match pe 304 turant, storage touch hi nahi hota.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py::parse_range` aur `api/routes.py::get_object`. `LocalAdapter.get` seek + bounded read (`remaining = end - start + 1`), `S3Adapter.get` `Range=f'bytes={start}-{end}'`. Test `test_range_requests_and_conditional_get`: `bytes=100-199` -> 206 + exact slice, `bytes=-10` -> last 10, `bytes=99999-` -> 416, If-None-Match -> 304.
advantages: Storage se sirf zaroori bytes padhe jaate hain
disadvantages: Zero-byte object pe koi bhi range 416
common_mistakes: Range end ko exclusive samajhna (HTTP mein inclusive hai)
416 ki jagah 200 ke saath poora object bhej dena
304 response mein body bhejna

question: What does strong read-after-write consistency mean, and does this system provide it?
answer_hinglish:
Strong read-after-write ka matlab: jaise hi PUT ne 200 return kiya, uske baad koi bhi GET (kisi bhi client se, kisi bhi API instance se) naya version dekhega. Koi 'thodi der purana data dikh sakta hai' wala window nahi.

Haan, yeh system strong read-after-write deta hai, aur reason simple hai: metadata ka single source of truth Postgres hai, aur `put_object` 200 tabhi return karta hai jab metadata transaction COMMIT ho chuka. Next GET `head_object` se `is_latest` row padhta hai -- same primary database se -- toh naya row dikhega. Blob pehle hi durable likha ja chuka hai (bytes first), toh pointer milne ke baad bytes bhi milenge. Delete aur overwrite ke liye bhi yahi: delete marker commit ho gaya toh agla GET 404 dega.

Yeh baat mention karna achha hai ki AWS S3 bhi Dec 2020 se strongly consistent hai; pehle overwrite/delete eventually consistent the.

Lekin caveats hain. Pehla, agar hum listing ke liye read replicas lagayein (SYSTEM_DESIGN 10x plan), toh replica lag se listing thodi stale ho sakti hai -- tab GET by key primary se hi padhna chahiye. Doosra, CDN cache ke peeche public reads stale ho sakte hain jab tak TTL/invalidation na ho. Teesra, access-key secret cache (60s) consistency of data nahi, auth revocation ko delay karta hai. Interview mein main bolta hoon: 'strong consistency humne isliye free mein payi kyunki metadata ek ACID database mein hai; sharding/replicas aate hi isko consciously design karna padega.'
why_needed: Clients (pipelines, apps) PUT ke turant baad GET karte hain; agar purana data mile toh subtle bugs aate hain. Consistency guarantee clear honi chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Bank passbook: deposit ki receipt mili (200) toh kisi bhi branch se balance check karo, deposit dikhega -- kyunki sab branches ek hi central ledger padhti hain.
how_it_works: Write: blob durable -> metadata COMMIT -> 200. Read: metadata (is_latest) -> blob. Kyunki commit visibility atomic hai aur sab instances ek Postgres padhte hain, response ke baad ka har read naya state dekhta hai.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` Consistency section: 'metadata commits before the 200'. Code: `put_object` mein `async with sm() as s, s.begin(): ... commit_version(...)` block complete hone ke baad hi `PutResult` return hota hai; `head_object` `WHERE ... AND is_latest` padhta hai. API stateless hai (`DEPLOYMENT.md`), saari coordination Postgres mein.

# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (put_object)
info = await storage.put(blob_key, stream)          # 1. bytes durable first
_verify_digests(info, content_md5, sha256_header, signed_sha256)
async with sm() as s, s.begin():                    # 2. metadata commit
    await s.execute(text(key_lock_sql()), {...})
    vid = await commit_version(s, bucket, key, ...)
return PutResult(vid, info.md5, info.size, info.sha256)   # 3. only now 200

Koi special 'wait and retry' logic nahi chahiye
Free mila kyunki metadata ACID DB mein hai
disadvantages: Single metadata DB scaling limit ban jata hai
Replicas/caches add karte hi guarantee weak ho sakti hai
common_mistakes: 200 metadata commit se pehle bhej dena
Read replicas se GET by key serve karna aur strong consistency claim karna
CDN-cached reads ko consistent maan lena

question: Why does this design split metadata (Postgres) from data (storage adapter)?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki dono ki requirements bilkul alag hain. Metadata chhota hai lekin uspe complex operations hote hain: 'is key ka latest version kaunsa hai', prefix listing, versions, ACL check, quota sum, lifecycle queries with window functions, multipart part tracking. Iske liye transactions, constraints aur indexes chahiye -- Postgres perfect hai. Data (bytes) bada hai, opaque hai, aur uspe sirf put/get/delete chahiye -- iske liye cheap, durable blob store best hai (local disk ya S3-compatible: SeaweedFS, MinIO, AWS S3).

Is split ke concrete fayde mere project mein: 'one latest version per key' DB ka partial unique index enforce karta hai (code bug ho tab bhi). Versioning flip, delete marker, quota check -- sab ek short ACID transaction mein. Renames/metadata changes bytes ko touch nahi karte. Aur storage backend pluggable hai -- `OBJ_STORAGE_BACKEND=local|s3` -- same API, same tests.

Cost bhi hai: do systems ek saath consistent rakhne padte hain. Crash ke beech mein state alag ho sakti hai -- isliye write order 'bytes first, metadata second' rakha, aur GC orphan blobs saaf karta hai. Backups bhi dono ke saath lene padte hain kyunki blob keys random hain -- metadata ke bina blob store sirf random naam wale files ka dher hai.

Real systems bhi yahi karte hain: S3 internally metadata index aur storage nodes alag rakhta hai, Ceph RGW bucket index alag rakhta hai.
why_needed: Bytes aur metadata ki access patterns, size aur consistency needs alag hain; ek hi system dono ke liye optimal nahi hota.
real_world_analogy: Library ka catalog (card index: title, author, shelf number) alag register mein hai aur books godown mein. Book dhundhne ke liye pehle catalog dekho; catalog mein entry tabhi banti hai jab book shelf pe rakh di gayi ho.
how_it_works: PUT: adapter mein random blob key ke naam se bytes -> Postgres row jisme blob_key pointer. GET: Postgres se row (latest/versionId) -> adapter se blob_key stream. Delete/overwrite: row change + blob_deletions queue -> GC adapter se delete.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py` ka module docstring yahi explain karta hai. `objects.blob_key` column 'random id in the storage adapter; NEVER derived from key'. `storage/base.py::StorageAdapter` protocol (put/get/delete/exists/list_older_than) do implementations ke saath: `storage/local.py`, `storage/s3.py`. `main.py::make_storage` backend choose karta hai. `ARCHITECTURE.md` Key decision 1.
disadvantages: Do systems ka consistency problem (orphans, GC)
common_mistakes: Bytes ko Postgres bytea mein rakhna (DB bloat, slow backups)
Metadata ko blob store ke object tags mein rakhna aur fir listing/transactions ki ummeed
Blob key ko object key se derive karna

question: Why are blob keys random instead of being derived from the object key?
answer_hinglish:
Teen solid reasons hain: security, flexibility, aur crash safety.

Security: object key user input hai -- `../../etc/passwd`, `\windows\path`, emoji, `%25`, kuch bhi. Agar hum key se file path banate (`root/bucket/key`), toh path traversal ka khatra hota aur har OS ke filename rules (length, reserved names, case-insensitivity on Windows) handle karne padte. Random hex blob key (`uuid4().hex + uuid4().hex[:8]`) ka matlab user ka string kabhi filesystem path tak pahunchta hi nahi. Local adapter defence in depth ke liye `_path` mein `blob_key.isalnum()` check bhi karta hai. Test `test_hostile_keys_never_touch_filesystem_paths` assert karta hai ki har file `blobs/` ke andar hai aur naam alphanumeric hai.

Flexibility: har write naya blob hai, toh overwrite kabhi existing bytes ko modify nahi karta -- readers purana blob padh rahe ho toh unke neeche se file nahi badalti. Versions natural hain: har version alag blob. 'Rename' metadata-only ho sakta hai (yahan implement nahi, lekin design allow karta hai).

Crash safety: kyunki naya blob alag naam pe likha jata hai, failed/half upload purane object ko kabhi corrupt nahi karta. Metadata commit hi 'switch' hai.

Cost: ek indirection (key -> blob_key lookup) aur blob store bina database ke unreadable hai -- backup dono ka saath chahiye. Dedupe bhi automatic nahi hota (same content do baar = do blobs).
why_needed: User-controlled strings ko filesystem/storage paths se alag rakhna ek basic security principle hai; plus write path immutable aur crash-safe banta hai.
real_world_analogy: Cloakroom token: aap coat dete ho, aapko random number wala token milta hai. Coat aapke naam se nahi rakha jata -- isliye koi 'mera naam ../../manager ka locker' bol ke kuch nahi kar sakta.

Client side `signing.py::quote_key` dot segments ko `%2E` encode karta hai taaki URL normalisation key ko na badle. Test: `test_hostile_keys_never_touch_filesystem_paths`.

def new_blob_key() -> str:
    return uuid.uuid4().hex + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]

def _path(self, blob_key: str) -> Path:
    if not blob_key.isalnum():          # defence in depth: keys are server-generated hex
        raise ValueError("invalid blob key")
    return self.root / blob_key[:2] / blob_key[2:4] / blob_key

question: Why does the write path store bytes first and commit metadata second?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki do systems ke beech atomic transaction nahi hai, toh humein choose karna padta hai ki crash pe kaunsi 'galat' state bachegi -- aur hum woh choose karte hain jo harmless ho.

Bytes first, metadata second: agar blob likhne ke baad aur COMMIT se pehle process crash ho, toh ek orphan blob bachta hai -- storage mein bytes hain jinko koi metadata point nahi karta. Yeh sirf wasted space hai; koi client usse dekh nahi sakta. GC grace period ke baad isko delete kar deta hai.

Ulta order socho: pehle metadata commit, phir bytes. Crash beech mein hua toh metadata ek aise blob ko point karega jo exist hi nahi karta -- dangling pointer. Har GET 500 dega, listing mein object dikhega lekin padhega nahi. Yeh user-visible corruption hai, aur detect karna bhi mushkil. Isliye ulta order bahut bura hai.

Yahi principle delete pe bhi lagta hai, ulti direction mein: pehle metadata hatao (row delete / is_latest flip + blob_deletions mein queue), phir bytes baad mein delete karo. Kabhi aisa moment nahi aata jab metadata ho lekin bytes na hon.

Mere `put_object` mein yeh bilkul explicit hai, aur failure pe cleanup bhi: digest mismatch, quota exceeded ya koi bhi exception -> `except BaseException: await storage.delete(blob_key)` (best effort; fail ho toh GC pakad lega). Yeh 'garbage allowed, dangling never' rule poore design ka backbone hai.
why_needed: Multi-store writes mein distributed transaction na ho toh ordering hi crash safety ka tool hai.
real_world_analogy: Pehle saaman godown ki shelf pe rakho, phir register mein entry karo. Beech mein bijli gayi toh shelf pe ek unregistered box milega (audit mein hata do). Ulta kiya toh register mein entry hai lekin shelf khaali -- customer aayega aur kuch nahi milega.
how_it_works: 1) Stream to new random blob (koi lock nahi). 2) Digests verify. 3) Short DB txn: advisory lock -> (quota) -> commit_version -> COMMIT. 4) 200. Failure ke kisi bhi step pe naya blob delete; crash pe orphan -> GC.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py` module docstring ('Write path ordering (crash safety)') aur `put_object`. `ARCHITECTURE.md` sequence diagram 'crash between blob write and COMMIT = orphan blob, removed by GC after grace period'. `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` #3 aur #15 (S3 unreachable -> 500 before metadata changes). Test: `test_gc_deletes_queued_and_orphan_blobs_but_keeps_live_ones` crash simulate karta hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py (put_object)
blob_key = new_blob_key()
info = await storage.put(blob_key, HashingStream(body, max_bytes))   # bytes first
try:
    _verify_digests(info, content_md5, sha256_header, signed_sha256)
    async with sm() as s, s.begin():                                 # metadata second
        ...
        vid = await commit_version(s, bucket, key, blob_key=blob_key, ...)
except BaseException:
    await storage.delete(blob_key)   # nothing references it; best effort (GC catches failures)
    raise
disadvantages: Storage temporarily zyada use hota hai
common_mistakes: Metadata pehle insert karke 'pending' flag ke bina bytes likhna
Failure pe blob cleanup bhool jana
Delete pe pehle bytes delete karna phir metadata

question: What is an orphan blob, and how does GC remove orphans without deleting in-flight uploads?
answer_hinglish:
Orphan blob woh hai jo blob store mein hai lekin koi metadata row (objects ya multipart_parts) usse reference nahi karti. Yeh aata hai jab process blob likhne ke baad aur metadata COMMIT se pehle crash ho jaye, ya failure pe best-effort `storage.delete` khud fail ho jaye, ya local adapter mein crash se `.tmp-*` file reh jaye.

GC (`run_gc`) ka doosra phase orphans dhundhta hai: `storage.list_older_than(orphan_grace_seconds)` -- sirf woh blobs jo grace period (default 3600s) se purane hain -- phir DB se saare referenced blob_keys ka set leta hai (objects UNION multipart_parts), aur jo candidate set mein nahi hai usse `delete_any` karta hai.

Grace period kyun zaroori hai? Kyunki 'unreferenced' ka matlab 'orphan' nahi hota. Ek upload abhi chal raha ho sakta hai: blob likha ja chuka, metadata commit hone wala hai. Agar GC usi waqt chale aur sirf 'unreferenced' dekhe, toh woh in-flight blob delete kar dega -- aur fir commit hoga, metadata dangling blob ko point karega. Ulta wahi bug jo bytes-first order se bachana tha! Grace period ensure karta hai ki sirf woh unreferenced blobs delete hon jo itne purane hain ki unka upload definitely khatam/mar chuka hai.

Tests: `test_gc_respects_grace_period_for_in_flight_uploads` ek fresh uncommitted blob likhta hai aur check karta hai GC usse nahi chhoota. `test_gc_deletes_queued_and_orphan_blobs_but_keeps_live_ones` mtime ko 2 ghante peeche karke orphan delete hone ka proof deta hai. Rule: grace period sabse lambe possible upload se bada hona chahiye (5 GiB slow client!).
why_needed: Bytes-first ordering garbage chhodta hai; bina safe GC ke storage leak hoti rahegi, aur galat GC data corrupt kar dega.
real_world_analogy: Godown audit: register mein entry nahi wale boxes hatao -- lekin sirf woh jo ek ghante se pade hain. Jo box abhi abhi truck se utra aur clerk entry likh raha hai, usse mat uthao.
how_it_works: Phase 2 of run_gc: candidates = blobs with mtime/LastModified < now - grace. referenced = set(objects.blob_key UNION multipart_parts.blob_key). delete candidates - referenced. Local adapter `list_older_than` `*/*/*` glob karta hai (including `.tmp-*`), S3 adapter `list_objects_v2` paginate karta hai.
in_this_project: `services/maintenance.py::run_gc`, `config.py` `orphan_grace_seconds: int = 3600  # GC never deletes blobs younger than this`, `storage/local.py::list_older_than` aur `delete_any`. Worker har 300s chalata hai (`worker.py`). Orphans milne pe `log.warning('gc_removed_orphan_blobs', extra={'count': orphans})`. Observation: yeh scan poore blob store ko list karta hai aur saare referenced keys memory mein laata hai -- bahut bade store pe scale nahi karega.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/maintenance.py (run_gc, orphan phase)
candidates = await storage.list_older_than(orphan_grace_seconds)
async with sm() as s:
    referenced = set((await s.execute(text(
        "SELECT blob_key FROM objects WHERE blob_key IS NOT NULL UNION "
        "SELECT blob_key FROM multipart_parts"))).scalars().all())
for name in candidates:
    if name not in referenced:
        await storage.delete_any(name)
        orphans += 1
advantages: Grace period in-flight uploads ko bachata hai
disadvantages: Grace galat set kiya toh data loss risk
common_mistakes: Grace period ko lambe uploads se chhota rakhna
Sirf 'unreferenced' check karke delete karna
Referenced set candidates se pehle padhna (race window badhta hai)

question: Why are blob deletions queued in a blob_deletions table instead of deleting inline?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki request ka success aur latency blob store ke delete pe depend nahi karna chahiye. Jab object overwrite hota hai (unversioned), permanently version delete hota hai, multipart part replace hota hai, ya upload abort/complete hota hai, toh purana blob unreferenced ho jata hai. Hum usse usi transaction mein `INSERT INTO blob_deletions (blob_key) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` karte hain, aur maintenance worker ka GC baad mein actual delete karta hai.

Fayde: (1) Atomicity -- 'metadata change' aur 'yeh blob ab delete karna hai' ek hi DB transaction mein record hote hain. Agar inline delete karte aur commit fail hota, toh humne live object ke bytes delete kar diye hote. Agar commit ke baad delete karte aur process crash hota, toh blob leak. Queue dono se bachata hai. (2) Latency -- S3 delete ek network call hai; request path pe nahi chahiye. (3) Reliability -- blob store slow/down ho tab bhi DELETE request succeed hoti hai; GC retry karega.

GC phase 1 extra safety ke saath chalta hai: har queued blob ke liye check karta hai ki koi objects ya multipart_parts row abhi bhi usse reference toh nahi karti (`still_used`), tabhi delete. Phir queue row hatata hai.

Trade-off: storage turant free nahi hota; aur agar worker band hai toh queue badhti rahegi -- `DEPLOYMENT.md` bolta hai 'alert if blob_deletions grows'. Review fix: pehle queued blobs pe koi grace nahi thi, toh overwrite se pehle shuru hua lamba GET GC run ke beech toot sakta tha; ab GC sirf `queued_at < now() - deletion_grace_seconds` (default 300s) wale blobs delete karta hai.
why_needed: Request path ko external storage ke deletes se decouple karna aur metadata change ke saath deletion intent ko atomically record karna.
real_world_analogy: Office mein shredding: aap file ko 'to shred' tray mein daal dete ho (register mein entry ke saath), shredder wala shaam ko sab ek saath shred karta hai. Aapko machine ke paas khade hone ki zaroorat nahi.
how_it_works: `_queue_blob_deletion` metadata txn ke andar insert karta hai. `run_gc` phase 1: `SELECT blob_key FROM blob_deletions ORDER BY queued_at LIMIT 10000` -> har ek ke liye reference re-check -> `storage.delete` -> queue row delete.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py::_queue_blob_deletion` (callers: `commit_version`, `delete_object`, `upload_part`, `complete_multipart`, `abort_multipart`). Table `blob_deletions (blob_key PK, queued_at)` migration mein comment ke saath: 'so the request path never waits on (or fails because of) blob deletion'. `services/maintenance.py::run_gc` phase 1. Test: `test_concurrent_writes_to_same_key` -> 19 overwritten blobs queued.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: objstore/services/objects.py + maintenance.py
async def _queue_blob_deletion(s, blob_key):
    if blob_key:
        await s.execute(text("INSERT INTO blob_deletions (blob_key) VALUES (:b) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"), {"b": blob_key})

# run_gc phase 1
still_used = await s.scalar(text("SELECT 1 FROM objects WHERE blob_key = :b UNION ALL "
                                 "SELECT 1 FROM multipart_parts WHERE blob_key = :b LIMIT 1"), {"b": b})
if not still_used:
    await storage.delete(b)

Blob store outage mein bhi delete requests succeed
disadvantages: Space der se free hota hai
Queued blobs deletion_grace_seconds (300s) tak extra space lete hain
common_mistakes: Commit se pehle blob delete karna
Queue ko transaction ke bahar likhna
Queue growth ko monitor na karna

question: How does bucket versioning work: the null version, enabled, and suspended?
answer_hinglish:
Bucket ke teen versioning states hain, S3 ki tarah: disabled (default), enabled, suspended. Ek baar enable kiya toh wapas disabled nahi ho sakta -- sirf suspended (API `VersioningIn` pattern sirf `enabled|suspended` allow karta hai).

Disabled: har key ka sirf ek row hota hai jiska version_id literal string `'null'` hai. Overwrite pe purana null row delete hota hai, naya insert hota hai, aur purana blob deletion queue mein jaata hai.

Enabled: har PUT naya `uuid4().hex` version id leta hai aur naya row insert hota hai; purane latest ko `is_latest = false`. Kuch delete nahi hota -- saare versions `?versionId=` se readable. DELETE bina versionId ke ek delete marker version banata hai (data abhi bhi hai).

Suspended: naye writes phir se `'null'` version id use karte hain -- agar pehle se koi null version hai toh woh replace hota hai -- lekin purane real versions (uuid wale) bach jaate hain. Yeh S3 behaviour hai: suspend karne se history delete nahi hoti.

Yeh sab `commit_version` mein hai: enabled branch vs else (disabled/suspended) branch. Test `test_versioning_and_delete_markers` v1, v2 likhta hai, versionId se v1 padhta hai, delete marker, undelete, aur permanent delete ke baad promotion check karta hai. Ek important consequence: versioned bucket mein 'delete' space free nahi karta -- isliye quota saare versions count karta hai aur lifecycle `noncurrent_expiration_days` chahiye.
why_needed: Accidental overwrite/delete se recovery aur audit history; S3-compatible semantics clients expect karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Google Docs version history: enabled = har save ka snapshot. Suspended = ab se sirf ek 'scratch' copy overwrite hoti rahegi, lekin purane snapshots history mein rahenge.
how_it_works: `commit_version` bucket['versioning'] dekhta hai. Enabled: new id + flip current. Else: version_id='null'; existing null row delete (+ blob queue); agar current latest null row nahi tha toh usse is_latest=false; phir insert as latest.

Migration: `versioning IN ('disabled','enabled','suspended')`. Test: `test_versioning_and_delete_markers`.
disadvantages: Delete se space free nahi hota
common_mistakes: Versioned bucket mein DELETE ko permanent samajhna
Suspended ko disabled samajhna
Lifecycle noncurrent rule ke bina versioning on karna

question: What is a delete marker, and how do you 'undelete' an object?
answer_hinglish:
Versioned bucket mein DELETE (bina versionId ke) data delete nahi karta. Woh ek naya version insert karta hai jiska `is_delete_marker = true`, size 0, koi blob nahi -- aur yeh marker latest ban jata hai. Ab GET bina versionId ke 404 deta hai header `x-obj-delete-marker: true` ke saath, aur listing mein key nahi dikhti (listing index `NOT is_delete_marker` filter karta hai). Lekin purane versions waise hi pade hain aur `?versionId=` se readable hain.

Undelete: delete marker bhi ek version hai jiska apna version_id hai. Us marker version ko permanently delete karo -- `DELETE ...?versionId=<marker_id>`. `delete_object` us row ko hatata hai, aur kyunki woh latest tha, sabse naya bacha hua version (`ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1`) phir se `is_latest = true` ban jata hai. Object wapas aa gaya!

Test `test_versioning_and_delete_markers` yahi poora flow chalata hai: v1, v2 put -> delete -> 404 with marker header -> versions listing mein `(marker latest, v2, v1)` -> marker version delete -> GET deta hai v2 -> v2 permanently delete -> GET deta hai v1.

Cost side: markers bhi rows hain, aur agar saare real versions expire ho jaayein toh ek 'lone delete marker' bachta hai jo bekaar hai -- lifecycle `run_lifecycle` aise markers hata deta hai ('expired object delete marker' S3 term).
why_needed: Versioning ka main purpose accidental delete se bachana hai; delete marker woh mechanism hai jo delete ko reversible banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Recycle bin: file delete karne pe woh bin mein chali jaati hai (marker), desktop pe nahi dikhti. Bin se 'restore' karo (marker hatao) aur file wapas.
how_it_works: Delete marker = `commit_version(..., blob_key=None, size=0, delete_marker=True)`. `head_object` latest row dekhta hai; agar marker hai toh NotFound with headers. Version delete pe agar `row.is_latest` tha toh promotion query chalti hai.
in_this_project: `services/objects.py::delete_object` (enabled/suspended branch -> `commit_version(..., delete_marker=True)`), `head_object` (`x-obj-delete-marker: true`), promotion: `UPDATE objects SET is_latest = true WHERE id = (SELECT id ... ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1)`. `services/maintenance.py::run_lifecycle` lone markers delete karta hai. Test: `test_versioning_and_delete_markers`.

# real, trimmed: tests/test_objects.py (test_versioning_and_delete_markers)
d = (await a.delete("photos", "doc.txt")).json()
assert d["delete_marker"] is True
gone = await a.get("photos", "doc.txt")
assert gone.status_code == 404 and gone.headers["x-obj-delete-marker"] == "true"
# "undelete": remove the delete marker version -> v2 is current again
await a.delete("photos", "doc.txt", version_id=d["version_id"])
assert (await a.get("photos", "doc.txt")).content == b"v2"

Undelete ke liye purana version copy karna (marker hatana kaafi hai)
Marker ka version_id ignore karna

question: What is a multipart upload and why does it exist?
answer_hinglish:
Multipart upload ek bada object chhote parts mein upload karne ka protocol hai. Problem: 5 GB file ek single PUT mein bhejo aur 99% pe connection toot jaye toh poora 5 GB dobara. Multipart mein: (1) `POST /buckets/b/uploads/key` se upload_id lo, (2) har part alag `PUT .../multipart/{upload_id}/parts/{n}` -- parallel bhej sakte ho, fail hua toh sirf woh part retry, (3) `POST .../complete` with part numbers + ETags ki list -- server unhe order mein jod ke ek object bana deta hai. (4) Ya `DELETE` se abort.

Rules S3 jaise hain: part number 1..10000 (DB CHECK bhi), har part (last ko chhod ke) kam se kam 5 MiB (`min_part_bytes`), complete mein parts ascending order mein bina duplicates ke, aur har ETag stored part se match hona chahiye. Same part number dobara upload karo toh replace hota hai (retry semantics) aur purane part ka blob deletion queue mein jaata hai.

Kyun min 5 MiB? Taaki 10000 parts * 5 MiB se bade objects ban sakein aur per-part overhead (metadata rows, requests) control mein rahe. Kyun complete pe ETag list? Taaki client explicitly bataye kaunse exact bytes chahiye -- agar beech mein kisi ne part replace kiya toh mismatch pakda jaye.

Gotcha: final ETag = `md5(concat(part md5s)) + '-N'`, object ka MD5 nahi. Aur bhoole hue uploads storage khaate hain lekin listing mein nahi dikhte -- lifecycle `abort_multipart_days` unhe saaf karta hai. Tests: `test_multipart_upload`, `test_multipart_min_part_size_and_abort`, `test_lifecycle_aborts_stale_multipart`.
why_needed: Large uploads ko resumable, parallel aur failure-tolerant banana; network failures pe poora object dobara na bhejna pade.
real_world_analogy: Ghar shift karna ek bade truck ki jagah kai chhote tempo mein: har tempo alag nikle, ek ka tyre puncture ho toh sirf woh dobara bhejo; end mein sab saman naye ghar mein serial number ke order mein set karo.
how_it_works: Initiate -> multipart_uploads row. Upload part -> naya blob + multipart_parts row (upsert). Complete -> validation -> parts ko stream karke naya final blob -> objects row (commit_version) + upload row delete + part blobs queue. Abort -> upload row delete (parts cascade) + blobs queue.

Config `min_part_bytes = 5 * 1024 ** 2`, tests mein `min_part_bytes=5` ya 8 se override. Migration `part_number int NOT NULL CHECK (part_number BETWEEN 1 AND 10000)`. `seed.py` 5 MiB + 1000 byte parts ke saath demo karta hai.
advantages: Single PUT limit (5 GiB) se bade objects possible
common_mistakes: Abort ya lifecycle rule bhool jana
Parts ko out of order list karna
Small parts (< 5 MiB) bhejna jo last nahi hain

question: What is a presigned URL and what exactly does it authorize?
answer_hinglish:
Presigned URL ek normal URL hai jisme query params mein signature hai, taaki koi bina credentials ke (browser, third party, mobile app) ek specific operation kar sake ek limited time ke liye. Example: user ko profile photo upload karne dena, bina usse apna secret diye aur bina bytes ko apne app server se guzare.

Mere system mein `POST /presign {method, bucket, key, expires_in, version_id?}` ek URL deta hai: `/buckets/b/objects/key?X-Obj-Credential=...&X-Obj-Expires=<unix>&X-Obj-Signature=...`. Signature HMAC hai `METHOD \n path \n canonical query \n 'PRESIGNED' \n expires` ka, signer ke secret se. Toh yeh URL bound hai: (1) method -- GET URL se DELETE karo toh 401, (2) exact key/path -- `me.txt` ko `other.txt` karo toh 401, (3) expiry -- time nikla toh 401, (4) versionId agar diya. Max expiry 7 din (`max_presign_seconds`).

Sabse important rule: URL signer ki authority carry karta hai. Isliye `/presign` pehle check karta hai ki caller khud yeh action kar sakta hai (`authorize` READ ya WRITE) -- 'you can only presign what you can do yourself'. Bob alice ke bucket ka URL nahi bana sakta (403).

Leak ho jaye toh blast radius: sirf woh ek method + key, expiry tak. Jaldi kill karna ho toh signer ka access key revoke karo (60s cache ke baad). Test `test_presigned_urls` saare cases cover karta hai: anonymous GET works, DELETE 401, other key 401, expired 401, presigned PUT from browser works, bob presign 403.
why_needed: Credentials share kiye bina limited, time-bound delegation; aur bade uploads/downloads ko seedha client se karwana.
real_world_analogy: Movie ticket: specific show, specific seat, specific date. Kisi ko de do toh woh sirf wahi show dekh sakta hai, poore theatre ka pass nahi hai, aur show ke baad bekaar.
how_it_works: Server: authorize caller -> expires_at = now + expires_in -> HMAC(secret, method/path/query/PRESIGNED/expires) -> URL. Verify: `X-Obj-Signature` present -> expiry check -> secret lookup -> recompute over actual request method/raw path/query -> `compare_digest`.
in_this_project: `services/signing.py::presign` aur `presigned_string`, `services/auth.py::_presigned`, `api/routes.py::presign` (`PresignIn`, `max_presign_seconds` check, `authorize(s, c, body.bucket, action)`). URL `cfg.public_base_url` se prefix hota hai. Test: `test_presigned_urls`. Review fix: 7-day max pehle sirf `/presign` route pe enforce hota tha (secret wala khud lamba URL bana sakta tha); ab `_presigned` use time pe bhi `exp > now + max + 60s` reject karta hai (`test_presigned_url_with_excessive_expiry_is_rejected_at_use`).

def presign(access_key, secret, method, raw_path, expires_at, extra_query=""):

question: Why is the ETag of a multipart upload not the MD5 of the object, and what does that mean for integrity?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki S3 multipart ETag ki definition hai `md5(part1_md5_binary || part2_md5_binary || ... ) + '-' + N`. Yaani parts ke MD5s ka MD5, aur suffix mein parts count. Poore object ka MD5 nahi.

Kyun aisa? Real S3 multipart completion mein parts ko server-side compose karta hai bina poore object ko dobara padhe -- toh poore object ka MD5 compute karne ka mauka hi nahi hota. Har part ka MD5 upload ke waqt pata tha, toh unka combination sasta hai. `-N` suffix clients ko signal karta hai 'yeh multipart ETag hai, isko MD5 mat samjho'.

Consequences: (1) Same bytes alag part sizes se upload karo toh ETag alag aayega -- content-equality check ke liye ETag unreliable. (2) `aws s3 sync` jaisi tools jo ETag ko local MD5 se compare karti hain, multipart objects pe galat 'changed' detect karti hain. (3) End-to-end integrity ke liye multipart ETag kaafi nahi.

Mere project mein: `complete_multipart` exactly S3 formula use karta hai, aur `test_multipart_upload` assert karta hai `expected_etag = md5(b''.join(md5(p).digest() for p in parts)).hexdigest() + '-3'`. Lekin kyunki mera completion parts ko re-stream karke naya blob likhta hai `HashingStream` ke through, mujhe poore object ka SHA-256 free mein mil jata hai -- jo `objects.sha256` mein store hota hai aur `x-obj-checksum-sha256` header mein return hota hai. `TRADEOFFS.md` #8: clients needing end-to-end integrity should use the SHA-256. Interview mein yeh classic gotcha hai -- 'ETag == MD5' sirf single PUT ke liye sach hai (aur SSE-KMS jaise cases mein S3 pe woh bhi nahi).
why_needed: Clients aur tools ETag pe integrity/sync decisions lete hain; galat assumption silent data issues ya bekaar re-uploads deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek kitaab ke har chapter ka fingerprint liya, phir un fingerprints ki list ka fingerprint banaya. Woh 'kitaab ka fingerprint' nahi hai -- agar chapters alag tarah se divide karo toh same kitaab ka alag number aayega.
how_it_works: upload_part har part ka md5 hex store karta hai. Complete pe `bytes.fromhex(p.etag)` binary digests concat -> md5 -> hexdigest + f'-{len(chosen)}'. Saath hi concatenated stream HashingStream se guzarta hai jo full-object sha256 deta hai.

question: How does HashingStream compute checksums and enforce the size limit while streaming in constant memory?
answer_hinglish:
`HashingStream` ek async iterator wrapper hai jo request body (`request.stream()`) aur storage adapter ke beech baithta hai. Har chunk jo aata hai: `self.size += len(chunk)`, agar size `max_bytes` se upar gaya toh turant `TooLarge` raise, warna `md5.update(chunk)`, `sha.update(chunk)`, aur chunk aage `yield`. Adapter us chunk ko disk/S3 pe likh deta hai, aur chunk memory se chala jata hai.

Isse teen cheezein milti hain ek hi pass mein. (1) Constant memory: 5 GiB object bhi aaye, memory mein ek time pe sirf ek chunk (+ adapter ka chhota buffer) hota hai -- kabhi poora object buffer nahi hota. (2) Checksums free: MD5 (ETag) aur SHA-256 dono streaming ke saath compute, dobara padhne ki zaroorat nahi. (3) Size limit enforcement while streaming: `Content-Length` header pe bharosa nahi kar sakte (chunked encoding mein hota hi nahi, ya client jhooth bol sakta hai). Isliye `put_object` pehle `content_length > max_bytes` pe early 413 deta hai (cheap), aur phir HashingStream actual bytes count karke limit enforce karta hai. Limit cross hui toh adapter ka exception handler temp file/upload saaf karta hai aur route 413 `EntityTooLarge` deta hai.

End mein `stream.info()` `BlobInfo(size, md5, sha256)` deta hai jo `_verify_digests` Content-MD5/SHA-256 headers se compare karta hai. Multipart completion bhi isi ko reuse karta hai: concatenated parts ka stream HashingStream se guzarta hai, toh final object ka size aur SHA-256 milta hai.
why_needed: Bade objects ko bina memory blow-up ke accept karna, aur integrity + limits ko ek hi pass mein enforce karna.
real_world_analogy: Paani ki pipeline mein meter aur filter: paani flow karta rehta hai (stream), meter litre ginta hai (size), quality sensor check karta hai (hash), aur limit cross hote hi valve band (TooLarge). Tanki mein poora paani jama nahi karna padta.
how_it_works: Async generator `__aiter__`: source ke chunks iterate, empty skip, count + check + hash update + yield. Adapter `async for chunk in stream` karta hai -- pull-based, toh backpressure natural hai: adapter slow likhe toh body bhi slow padha jayega.
in_this_project: `storage/base.py::HashingStream` aur `BlobInfo`. `put_object` mein `stream = HashingStream(body, max_bytes)`, `except TooLarge as exc: raise EntityTooLarge(str(exc))`. `config.py` `max_object_bytes = 5 * 1024 ** 3  # single PUT limit (S3: 5 GiB)`. Local adapter failure pe `tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)`. Tests: `test_put_get_roundtrip_metadata_and_etag` (ETag + SHA-256 header), `test_large_streaming_upload_over_8mb_uses_s3_multipart` (20MB stream).
code_example:
# real: objstore/storage/base.py
class HashingStream:
    def __init__(self, source, max_bytes):
        self.source, self.max = source, max_bytes
        self.md5, self.sha = hashlib.md5(), hashlib.sha256()
        self.size = 0

    async def __aiter__(self):
        async for chunk in self.source:
            if not chunk:
                continue
            self.size += len(chunk)
            if self.size > self.max:
                raise TooLarge(f"object exceeds {self.max} bytes")
            self.md5.update(chunk)
            self.sha.update(chunk)
            yield chunk

Content-Length pe bharosa kiye bina limit

question: Walk through what happens on PUT /buckets/{b}/objects/{key}, end to end.
answer_hinglish:
Main ise steps mein bolta hoon.

1. Route (`api/routes.py::put_object`): `authenticate` -- signed header verify (HMAC, clock skew, `x-obj-content-sha256`) ya presigned URL. `_check_key` -- key 1..1024 bytes. Short session mein `authorize(..., Action.WRITE)` -- owner/admin/write grant; bucket row (versioning, quota) milta hai. Session yahin band -- upload ke dauraan koi DB connection/lock nahi pakda jata.

2. `services/objects.py::put_object`: agar `Content-Length > max_bytes` toh turant 413. Naya random `blob_key`. `HashingStream(request.stream(), max_bytes)` adapter ko diya -- bytes stream hote hain, md5/sha256/size compute, limit enforce. Adapter atomically likhta hai (local: temp + fsync + rename; S3: boto3 managed upload).

3. `_verify_digests`: Content-MD5 (base64 -> hex) vs md5, `x-obj-checksum-sha256` vs sha256, aur signed payload hash (agar signature ne body hash cover kiya) vs sha256. Mismatch -> 400 BadDigest.

4. Short transaction: `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(bucket/key))` -- sirf same key ke writers serialize. Agar bucket pe quota hai toh bucket row `FOR UPDATE` + `_check_quota` (saare versions + pending parts). Phir `commit_version` -- versioning ke hisaab se flip/replace + INSERT latest row; replaced null blob queue mein. COMMIT.

5. Koi bhi exception step 3-4 mein -> `storage.delete(blob_key)` aur re-raise. Success -> 200 with `ETag`, `x-obj-version-id`, `x-obj-checksum-sha256`.

Key design points: lock window chhota (sirf metadata), bytes first, failure pe cleanup, aur strong read-after-write kyunki 200 commit ke baad.
why_needed: Yeh system ka core path hai; interviewer isi se judge karta hai ki aap crash safety, concurrency aur integrity ek saath samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Courier hub: pehle ID check (auth), phir parcel weigh + scan karte hue shelf pe rakho (stream + hash), label se match karo (digest), phir register mein ek line entry (short txn), receipt do (200). Gadbad hui toh parcel shelf se hatao.
how_it_works: Auth -> authz (short session) -> stream to new blob with hashing -> verify digests -> short txn (advisory lock, optional bucket lock + quota, commit_version) -> response. Error path deletes the new blob.

question: How does the local filesystem adapter make writes crash-safe, and why are directories sharded?
answer_hinglish:
Local adapter teen techniques use karta hai: temp file, fsync, atomic rename -- plus sharded directories.

Write flow (`LocalAdapter.put`): final path `root/ab/cd/<blob_key>` hai. Pehle same directory mein `.tmp-<uuid>` file kholte hain aur saare chunks usme likhte hain. End mein `_finish`: `flush()` (Python buffer -> OS), `os.fsync(fd)` (OS page cache -> disk), `close()`, aur `os.replace(tmp, final)`. `os.replace` same filesystem pe atomic rename hai -- reader ko ya toh koi file nahi dikhegi ya poori file; half-written blob kabhi us naam pe visible nahi hota. fsync rename se PEHLE isliye ki power-loss pe aisa na ho ki rename disk pe pahunch gaya lekin data nahi (file ka naam hai, content zero/garbage).

Failure: koi bhi exception (TooLarge, client disconnect, cancel) -> `f.close()` + `tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)`. Process hi crash ho jaye toh `.tmp-*` file bach jaati hai -- `list_older_than` `*/*/*` glob mein temp files bhi aati hain (wo kabhi referenced nahi hoti), toh GC grace ke baad unhe `delete_any` se hata deta hai.

Sharding: `blob_key[:2]/blob_key[2:4]/` -- 256 * 256 = 65536 directories. Ek directory mein millions of files ho toh lookup, listing, backup tools sab slow ho jaate hain (filesystem dependent). Random hex keys uniformly distribute hote hain, toh har directory chhoti rehti hai.

Performance: har chunk write `asyncio.to_thread` hop hai; maine open+mkdir ek hop, flush+fsync+close+rename ek hop mein group kiya ('fewer thread hops' TESTING.md mein PUT improvement ka ek part). Observation: parent directory fsync nahi hota after rename, toh Linux pe power-loss ke baad rename ki durability strictly guaranteed nahi.
why_needed: Disk pe 'ya toh poora ya kuch nahi' semantics aur bade numbers of blobs ke saath filesystem performance dono chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Exam answer sheet pehle rough copy pe likho (temp), check karo ki sab saaf likha hai (fsync), phir ek jhatke mein fair copy box mein daalo (rename). Box mein kabhi aadhi sheet nahi jaati. Aur sheets ko roll number ke pehle digits se alag drawers mein rakho (sharding).
how_it_works: tmp in same dir (rename atomic only within same filesystem) -> write chunks via threads -> flush -> fsync -> close -> os.replace. GET: open, seek(start), bounded reads of 256KB. Delete: unlink(missing_ok). GC: glob */*/* with mtime cutoff.

question: How does the S3 adapter stream an upload into boto3 with constant memory and backpressure?
answer_hinglish:
Problem: boto3 synchronous hai aur `upload_fileobj` ek file-like object se `read()` karna chahta hai, jabki hamare bytes ek async iterator (request body via HashingStream) se aa rahe hain. Poora object memory mein buffer karna option nahi (5 GiB).

Solution: `_QueueReader`, ek `io.RawIOBase` jo ek bounded chunk queue ke upar bana hai, `threading.Condition` ke saath. Do sides hain:

Producer (event loop side): `S3Adapter.put` `async for chunk in stream` karta hai aur har chunk `await asyncio.to_thread(reader.feed, chunk)` se daalta hai. `feed` block karta hai jab queue mein 8 se zyada chunks hon -- yeh backpressure hai: S3 slow hai toh hum client ka body bhi slow padhenge, memory nahi badhegi. Kyunki feed thread mein chalta hai, event loop block nahi hota.

Consumer (boto3 thread): `upload_fileobj(io.BufferedReader(reader), bucket, blob_key)` ek alag thread mein (`asyncio.to_thread` + `ensure_future`). boto3 `readinto` call karta hai jo queue se chunk nikalta hai, wait karta hai jab khaali ho, aur `finish()` ke baad 0 return karke EOF signal deta hai. boto3 khud 8MB se bade data pe managed multipart upload pe switch karta hai.

Errors: agar upstream stream fail ho (TooLarge, client disconnect), `reader.finish(exc)` -> `readinto` `IOError` raise karta hai -> boto3 upload abort hota hai; hum task await karke original exception re-raise karte hain. Isse koi committed half-blob nahi banta.

Proof: `test_large_streaming_upload_over_8mb_uses_s3_multipart` real SeaweedFS ke against 20MB upload karta hai aur SHA-256 match karta hai. Benchmarks: 64MB PUT 45 MB/s (S3 adapter, SeaweedFS in Docker) vs 153 MB/s local -- thread hops aur Docker networking ka cost.
why_needed: Async web server aur sync SDK ke beech bridge chahiye jo constant memory aur flow control maintain kare.
real_world_analogy: Conveyor belt jisme sirf 8 dabbe aa sakte hain: packing wala (event loop) dabbe rakhta hai, loading wala (boto3 thread) uthata hai. Belt bhar gayi toh packing wala ruk jaata hai -- godown mein dher nahi lagta.
how_it_works: Bounded producer-consumer with Condition variable: feed waits while len(chunks) > 8; readinto pops a chunk, notifies, copies into boto3's buffer, keeps remainder in _buf; finish sets closed flag + optional error. Download side: `get_object(Range=...)` aur `body.read(256KB)` in threads.

Tests: `tests/test_s3_adapter.py` -- `test_full_flow_on_s3_backend` aur `test_large_streaming_upload_over_8mb_uses_s3_multipart` (skipped agar endpoint down).

def feed(self, chunk: bytes) -> None:
    with self._cv:
        while len(self._chunks) > 8:          # backpressure: at most ~8 chunks buffered
            self._cv.wait()
        self._chunks.append(chunk)
        self._cv.notify_all()

async def put(self, blob_key, stream):
    reader = _QueueReader()
    task = asyncio.ensure_future(asyncio.to_thread(
        self.client.upload_fileobj, io.BufferedReader(reader), self.bucket, blob_key))
    try:
        async for chunk in stream:
            await asyncio.to_thread(reader.feed, chunk)
        reader.finish()
    except BaseException as exc:
        reader.finish(exc)
        ...
        raise
    await task
    return stream.info()
